lessons.title: Conducting a Hive Inspection
lessons.body: Inspecting a hive is like checking on a valuable but delicate friend. You want to know they are healthy and happy, but you don't want to disturb them too much. The best time to open a hive is on a warm, sunny day between 10am and 4pm, when most of the worker bees are out foraging. Avoid opening on windy, rainy, or very cold days. Wear protective clothing: a veil, gloves, and light-colored overalls. Use a smoker to calm the bees. Before you start, have your hive tool and a notebook ready. Stand to the side of the hive, not in front of the entrance, to avoid blocking the flight path. Give a few puffs of smoke at the entrance, wait 30 seconds, then lift the lid gently. Use your hive tool to pry it open. Work from the outside frames inward. Lift each frame slowly, keeping it over the hive to avoid dropping the queen. Look for signs of a healthy colony: eggs, larvae, capped brood, stored honey and pollen, and the queen. Check for pests, diseases, and swarm cells. Limit each inspection to 15-20 minutes to avoid stressing the bees. Close the hive carefully, ensuring no gaps. Record what you saw: date, time, weather, number of frames with brood, honey stores, queen seen (yes/no), and any problems. In Africa, many beekeepers use top-bar hives or Kenya Top Bar Hives (KTBH). The inspection method is similar, but you work with bars instead of frames. Always approach calmly and move slowly. If the bees become very aggressive, close the hive and try again another day. Regular inspections, every 7-10 days during the active season, help you catch problems early and keep your colony strong.

lessons.title: Reading Frames and Recognizing Queen Status
lessons.body: Reading frames is the skill of understanding what the bees are doing by looking at the comb. Each frame tells a story. You need to recognize the difference between eggs, larvae, and capped brood. Eggs are tiny, white, and stand upright at the bottom of cells. Larvae are white, curled, and lie in a pool of royal jelly. Capped brood is flat, biscuit-colored, and covers the cell. A healthy queen lays eggs in a tight pattern, often in the center of the frame. If you see eggs, you know the queen was there within the last three days. If you see larvae, she was there within the last nine days. If you see only capped brood, the queen may have stopped laying or is missing. The queen herself is longer than worker bees, with a pointed abdomen and shorter wings. She is usually surrounded by a circle of attendant bees. In Africa, local bee races like the African honey bee (Apis mellifera scutellata) are smaller and more defensive. Marking the queen with a small dot of paint (white, yellow, red, green, or blue) helps you find her quickly. If you cannot find the queen but see eggs, she is likely present. If you see no eggs and no larvae, the colony may be queenless. In that case, check for queen cells: peanut-shaped cells hanging from the comb. If you find queen cells, the colony is either swarming or replacing the queen. A laying worker can also occur in queenless colonies, but they only lay drone eggs, which are raised in larger cells. Knowing these signs helps you decide whether to requeen, add a frame of eggs from another hive, or leave the colony alone. Practice reading frames every inspection to build your confidence.

lessons.title: Detecting Pests and Diseases
lessons.body: Pests and diseases can weaken or kill your colony. Common pests in Africa include ants, termites, wax moths, small hive beetles, and varroa mites. Ants and termites can be controlled by placing the hive on stands with grease or oil barriers. Wax moths attack weak colonies, especially in stored combs. Keep your hive strong and remove unused combs. Small hive beetles are black, about 5mm long, and hide in corners. They can be trapped with oil traps or diatomaceous earth. Varroa mites are tiny, reddish-brown parasites that feed on bees. They are less common in Africa but can be a problem. Check for mites by using a sticky board or sugar shake method. Diseases include American foulbrood (AFB), European foulbrood (EFB), chalkbrood, and nosema. AFB causes sunken, perforated cappings and a foul smell. EFB causes twisted larvae that die before capping. Chalkbrood turns larvae into white, chalky mummies. Nosema causes dysentery and crawling bees. To detect diseases, inspect brood frames carefully. Look for discolored larvae, sunken cappings, or a bad smell. If you suspect AFB, burn the infected frames and sterilize your tools. For EFB, requeen and improve ventilation. Chalkbrood often clears up with better airflow and a stronger colony. Nosema can be treated with fumagillin, but prevention is better: keep hives dry and well-ventilated. Always maintain good hygiene: clean your hive tool between hives, and never exchange combs between sick and healthy colonies. Regular inspections help you spot problems early. If you see something unusual, take a photo and ask an experienced beekeeper or extension officer for advice. Early action saves colonies.

lessons.title: Managing Space: Adding Supers
lessons.body: Bees need space to store honey and raise brood. When a colony grows, it fills the brood chamber and may become crowded. This triggers swarming. To prevent swarming and increase honey production, you add supers. A super is a box placed on top of the brood chamber. It contains frames for honey storage. In Africa, many beekeepers use Langstroth hives with supers, or top-bar hives where you add more bars. The rule of thumb: when the brood chamber is 70-80% full, add a super. Check by looking at the frames: if 7 out of 10 frames are drawn and covered with bees, it's time. Add the super with frames that have foundation or starter strips. If you use a queen excluder, place it between the brood chamber and the super to keep the queen from laying in the honey super. However, some beekeepers avoid excluders because they can reduce honey yield. In Africa, African bees may be more reluctant to pass through excluders. Monitor the super: when the frames are 80% capped, add another super. You can add multiple supers, stacking them. Ensure the hive is level and stable. During a strong honey flow, bees can fill a super in 2-3 weeks. If you don't add space in time, the colony will swarm, and you lose half your bees. Conversely, adding too much space too early can stress the colony, as they must heat and defend a larger area. So add supers gradually. In top-bar hives, simply add more bars with guides. Always inspect the super every 7-10 days during the flow. Harvest honey only when frames are fully capped. Leave enough honey for the bees, especially before the dry season. Proper space management keeps your colony productive and healthy.

lessons.title: Dealing with Aggressive Colonies
lessons.body: Aggressive colonies are a common challenge, especially with African bee races. Aggressiveness can be genetic, environmental, or due to poor handling. Signs include bees following you, stinging without provocation, and boiling out of the hive when opened. First, check your own behavior: move slowly, wear clean, light-colored clothing, and avoid crushing bees. Use smoke gently. If a colony remains aggressive, consider requeening. Order a gentle queen from a reputable breeder. To requeen, find and kill the old queen, then introduce the new queen in a cage. Leave her caged for 2-3 days, then release her. Alternatively, you can split the aggressive colony and let them raise a new queen from eggs from a gentle colony. Another method is to move the aggressive hive to a new location, at least 3 km away, and place a gentle colony in its old spot. The foragers will join the gentle colony. If you cannot requeen, manage the colony defensively: work in the late afternoon when bees are calmer, use plenty of smoke, and keep inspections short. Wear extra protection: a thick suit, gloves, and boots. Never work an aggressive colony near people or animals. If the colony is too dangerous, consider destroying it by pouring soapy water into the hive. This is a last resort. In Africa, many beekeepers use local bees that are naturally aggressive. Some choose to work with them because they are productive and resistant to pests. But if you have neighbours or livestock, a gentle colony is safer. Always inform your neighbours before inspecting an aggressive hive. With patience and proper management, you can reduce aggression and make beekeeping enjoyable.

lessons.title: Seasonal Maintenance Tasks
lessons.body: Beekeeping follows the seasons. In Africa, seasons vary: wet and dry, or hot and cool. Your maintenance tasks should match the bees' needs. During the rainy season, ensure hives are dry and well-ventilated. Check for leaks and repair them. Raise hives on stands to prevent flooding and ant attacks. In the dry season, bees may need water. Provide a shallow water source with stones or sticks so bees don't drown. Also, watch for absconding due to lack of forage. If nectar is scarce, feed sugar syrup (1:1 sugar to water) to keep the colony alive. In hot regions, provide shade for the hive. In cool regions, reduce the entrance to keep warmth in. During the honey flow, add supers as needed and inspect weekly. After harvest, leave enough honey for the bees. In areas with a cold season, insulate the hive with grass or leaves, and reduce the entrance. In all seasons, keep the apiary clean: remove tall grass, and control pests. Check hives monthly during low activity. Replace old, dark combs with fresh foundation to reduce disease. Repair or replace damaged hive parts. In Africa, many beekeepers use locally available materials: mud, thatch, or metal sheets for roofs. Ensure the hive is predator-proof: use wire mesh to keep out honey badgers and monkeys. Record everything: date, tasks done, observations. This helps you plan for the next season. Remember, bees are resilient but need your help to thrive. By following a seasonal calendar, you keep your colonies strong and productive year-round.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to inspect a beehive?
options: B) Between 10am and 4pm on a sunny day
quiz.explanation: Most worker bees are out foraging during the warm, sunny part of the day, making the hive calmer and easier to inspect.

quiz.q: Why should you stand to the side of the hive when inspecting?
options: A) To avoid blocking the bees' flight path
B) To get a better view of the frames
C) To prevent the queen from escaping
D) To stay out of the sun
quiz.explanation: Standing in front of the entrance blocks foraging bees and can agitate the colony.

quiz.q: How long should a hive inspection ideally last?
quiz.explanation: Keeping inspections short (15-20 minutes) minimizes stress on the bees and reduces the chance of robbing.

quiz.q: What tool is used to calm bees during inspection?
quiz.explanation: Smoke masks alarm pheromones and triggers a feeding response, making bees less defensive.

quiz.q: What should you record after each inspection?
options: A) Date, time, weather, brood, honey, queen seen, problems
B) Only the number of bees
C) The color of the hive
quiz.explanation: Detailed records help track colony health and identify trends over time.

quiz.q: What does the presence of eggs indicate?
options: B) The queen was there within the last 3 days
C) The hive is about to swarm
quiz.explanation: Eggs hatch into larvae after about 3 days, so their presence confirms recent queen activity.

quiz.q: How can you tell a queen bee apart from worker bees?
options: A) She is smaller and darker
B) She has a longer, pointed abdomen and shorter wings
D) She is always on the honey frames
quiz.explanation: The queen's elongated abdomen and shorter wings distinguish her from workers.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of marking the queen?
options: A) To make her lay more eggs
B) To easily identify her during inspections
quiz.explanation: A marked queen is easier to spot, saving time and reducing disturbance.

quiz.q: What does a tight brood pattern indicate?
quiz.explanation: A tight pattern means the queen is laying eggs consistently and the brood is developing well.

quiz.q: If you see queen cells, what might be happening?
options: A) The colony is preparing to swarm or replace the queen
B) The bees are making honey
C) The hive is too cold
D) The queen is laying eggs
quiz.explanation: Queen cells are built for swarming or supersedure (replacing an old or failing queen).

quiz.q: Which pest can be controlled by placing hive stands in oil?
quiz.explanation: Oil barriers on hive stands prevent ants and other crawling insects from reaching the hive.

quiz.q: What is a sign of American foulbrood (AFB)?
options: A) Sunken, perforated cappings and a foul smell
quiz.explanation: AFB causes sunken, perforated cappings and a distinctive foul odor.

quiz.q: How can you detect varroa mites?
options: A) By looking at the honey
B) Using a sticky board or sugar shake method
C) By listening to the hive
quiz.explanation: Sticky boards and sugar shakes are common methods to monitor varroa mite levels.

quiz.q: What is a common treatment for chalkbrood?
quiz.explanation: Chalkbrood often resolves with better airflow and a stronger colony.

quiz.q: Why should you clean your hive tool between hives?
quiz.explanation: Disease spores can be transferred on tools, so cleaning prevents cross-contamination.

quiz.q: When should you add a super to a hive?
options: A) When the brood chamber is 70-80% full
B) At the start of winter
C) When the bees are aggressive
quiz.explanation: Adding a super when the brood chamber is nearly full gives bees space and prevents swarming.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a queen excluder?
options: A) To keep the queen from laying in honey supers
B) To keep the queen in the brood chamber
quiz.explanation: A queen excluder allows workers to pass but excludes the larger queen from honey supers.

quiz.q: What can happen if you add a super too early?
options: A) The colony may become stressed
C) The honey will be bitter
D) The queen will stop laying
quiz.explanation: Too much space too soon forces bees to heat and defend a larger area, which can stress the colony.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect a super during a honey flow?
quiz.explanation: Regular checks ensure space is available and honey is capped properly.

quiz.q: What is a sign of an aggressive colony?
options: A) Bees following you and stinging without provocation
B) Bees fanning at the entrance
quiz.explanation: Aggressive colonies often follow and sting intruders unprovoked.

quiz.q: What is a method to reduce aggression in a colony?
options: A) Requeening with a gentle queen
quiz.explanation: Requeening with a gentle strain can reduce aggression genetically.

quiz.q: Why should you work an aggressive colony in the late afternoon?
options: B) More bees are out foraging
D) The queen is easier to find
quiz.explanation: Late afternoon often finds bees less defensive as they prepare for night.

quiz.q: What is a last resort for an extremely aggressive colony?
options: A) Destroying it with soapy water
B) Moving it to a new location
quiz.explanation: If a colony is too dangerous, destroying it may be necessary for safety.

quiz.q: What should you do during the rainy season to maintain hives?
options: A) Ensure hives are dry and well-ventilated
quiz.explanation: Damp hives can lead to disease, so keeping them dry is crucial.

quiz.q: Why provide a water source for bees in the dry season?
options: A) To prevent bees from absconding
quiz.explanation: Bees need water to dilute honey and cool the hive; lack of water can cause absconding.

quiz.q: What is a sign that bees may abscond in the dry season?
options: A) Lack of forage and dwindling stores
quiz.explanation: When nectar and pollen are scarce, bees may leave to find better conditions.

quiz.q: How can you protect hives from honey badgers?
options: B) Place hives on tall stands
quiz.explanation: Wire mesh around the hive can deter honey badgers and other predators.

quiz.q: Why replace old, dark combs?
quiz.explanation: Old combs can harbor pathogens and pesticides, so replacing them improves colony health.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for record-keeping in beekeeping?
options: A) Record date, tasks, and observations
C) Keep records in your head
quiz.explanation: Detailed records help you plan seasonal tasks and track colony performance.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect a disease but are unsure?
options: A) Ask an experienced beekeeper or extension officer
quiz.explanation: Getting expert advice prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatments.
